http://www.aina.org/news/20260807125903..text: Assyrian Patriarch Makes First Visit to Romania for Syriac Studies Congress By Aurelian Iftimiu https://basilica.ro Posted 2026-08-07 17:59 GMT His Holiness Mar Awa III, Catholicos-Patriarch of the Assyrian Church of the East. His Holiness Mar Awa III, Catholicos-Patriarch of the Assyrian Church of the East, made his first-ever visit to Romania from August 3 to 7. According to a press release from the Levant Institute, the visit took place in conjunction with the 14th World Congress for Syriac Studies and the 12th International Conference on Christian Arabic Studies, organised by the Levant Institute and the Romanian Academy at the Palace of the Parliament in Bucharest. The Patriarch participated in the congress alongside His Grace Mar Paulus Benjamin, Bishop of Chicago and the Eastern United States of the Assyrian Church of the East. About Patriarch Mar Awa III His Holiness is the 122nd Catholicos-Patriarch of the Assyrian Church of the East and the first primate of the Church to have been born in the diaspora, in Chicago, United States. The press release noted that his life story reflects the experience of Middle Eastern Christians over the past few decades. "The story of Mar Awa III is the story of an entire generation of Eastern Christians who were compelled to rebuild their lives far from the lands where they were born and received the gift of faith, while preserving a heritage nearly two millennia old." "He is not only the Patriarch of an ancient Church, but also a man whose biography embodies the journey of an entire community: Mesopotamia, the diaspora, the preservation of identity, and the memory of an endangered heritage," the press release noted. A bridge between East and West According to the same source, Patriarch Mar Awa III is promoting dialogue among Churches, advocates for the protection of the Christian heritage of the Near East, and supports historic Christian communities affected by conflicts in recent decades. His Holiness holds a doctorate in theology from the Pontifical Oriental Institute in Rome and is regarded as one of the leading contemporary scholars of the Syriac tradition. He has authored numerous works on the theology and spirituality of the Assyrian Church of the East. In a message issued ahead of the event, Patriarch Mar Awa III highlighted Romania's role in fostering dialogue between East and West. "These events send a very powerful message from the heart of the European Union. Historically, this message serves as a bridge between East and West, and Romania is one of the few countries within the European Union well-positioned to fulfil this important role," His Holiness said. The World Congress for Syriac Studies and the International Conference on Christian Arabic Studies will bring together scholars and representatives from leading universities and research institutes worldwide, providing a forum for academic and intercultural dialogue dedicated to Syriac and Arabic Christian heritage. The Assyrian Church of the East The Assyrian Church of the East traces its origins to the ancient Syriac Christian communities of Mesopotamia and links its foundation to the preaching of the Holy Apostle Thomas and his disciples, Saints Addai and Mari. During the first centuries of Christianity, the Church carried out extensive missionary work, reaching from Persia to India, Central Asia, and China. Following the Third Ecumenical Council of Ephesus in 431, the Assyrian Church of the East separated from the Orthodox Church, as it did not accept the council's decisions. Today, the headquarters of the Assyrian Church of the East is located in Ankawa, near Erbil, Iraq, while its faithful are spread across the Middle East, Europe, North America, and Australia. https://www.classicalcalifornia.org/arti.text: Find Us on Social Media articles / Brahms Saturday Morning Car Tunes: Johannes Brahms Berni Schoenfield/Getty Images Brahms the pop star? His melodies show up in movies, cartoons, even pop songs, because he loved popular music too! Tune in this week for a lullaby, a Hungarian dance, student drinking songs, and Frank Sinatra. Listen to the episode! Bettmann/Getty Images Howdy, howdy, howdy! I’m Solomon Reynolds , and this is: Saturday Morning Car Tunes ! This morning… Born in 1833, Johannes Brahms was a German Romantic composer who came after Beethoven , Schubert , and Schumann . As a kid, people say he played the piano in sailors’ bars to help earn money for his family. The folk and popular music he played there shows up in his own compositions. His Piano Sonata No. 1, which you're listening to right now, was inspired by both Beethoven and folk songs. Brahms studied the musical past but also looked toward what the future could sound like. He pushed the boundaries of Classical forms through variations, taking a melody and playing it as many ways as he could imagine. These are his V ariations on a Theme by Handel , which he called his “favorite work.” But Brahms wasn’t just good at writing piano variations. He could also handle a whole orchestra. His Variations on a Theme by Haydn was the first orchestral piece where he combined everything he’d learned from older composers into something new, genuinely his own. Because Brahms loved and collected so many folk songs, he got really good at writing melodies. You’ve probably already heard his most famous one. Brahms never wrote an opera—he could never find a libretto, or story, he liked. But many think his G erman Requiem is his greatest work. Instead of writing it in the traditional Latin, Brahms set the text in German, although he said it could be just called a “human” requiem. Critics raved, and the piece made Brahms a major European composer. When Hungarian refugees passed through Germany, Brahms met the violinist Ede Reményi, who taught him about the Hungarian style, a mix of Hungarian and Romani musics. The third movement of Brahms' Violin Concerto is his greatest work in the Hungarian style and was featured in the 2007 film, There Will Be Blood . In fact, film, TV, and pop culture love Brahms’s Hungarian music. His Hungarian Dance No. 5 shows up all over the place: in a Looney Tunes cartoon, a Charlie Chaplin movie, and even an episode of The Simpsons . One reason pop culture loves Brahms’s music so much is that Brahms himself borrowed from the pop music of his day. When the University of Breslau offered him an honorary doctorate, Brahms wrote his Academic Festival Overture for the occasion. The piece is packed with half a dozen popular tunes and songs the students would recognize. Brahms’ four symphonies were milestones in German music, some of the most important pieces written in the 19th century. His Third Symphony reached a new level of form, balance, and coherence. The third movement was so good, Frank Sinatra wrote it into his song, “Take My Love.” Brahms! He's the bombs dot coms. I’m Solomon Reynolds. I write and produce Saturday Morning Car Tunes with research assistant Carolina Correa and audio engineer Stephen Page, only on Classical California. Tune in—or out of your car—next Saturday morning! https://www.dw.com/en/czechia-braces-for.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5POMX Prefer DW on Google 'Strike — For a free press, free media' Many in Czechia fear that the government's plans to change the way public media is funded will undermine the independence of Czech Television and Czech Radio Image: Katerina Sulova/CTK Photo/IMAGO Advertisement Hundreds of thousands of people are expected to rally in Prague this weekend to protest the Czech government's bid to ram a bill to reform public media funding through parliament in a surprise overnight session late last month. The populist coalition of Prime Minister Andrej Babis fast-tracked the first of three readings of the legislation, which culminated in a vote of approval at 04:36 a.m. on October 24. The bill has already provoked numerous demonstrations and strikes across the country, but Sunday's gathering in the capital's Letna Park is likely to be by far the largest to date. What's in the bill? Under the government's proposal, the license fee model that currently funds Czech Television (CT) and Czech Radio (CRo) would be scrapped, and the broadcasters would be funded directly from the state budget. The three parties in the coalition — Babis's centrist ANO, the far-right SPD, and radical conservative Motorists, whose voter bases tend to be less affluent — insist that the license fee is an unfair tax. Crowds protested outside parliament while inside, the government pushed through the first reading of the controversial media funding bill on the night of October 23/24 Image: Michal Kamaryt/CTK Photo/IMAGO The parties argue that the new arrangement, which would see funding for CT and CRo cut by around 15% in the first year, would make the two more efficient. They also point out that several other European Union states have made similar changes. What are the objections to the bill? Critics have angrily dismissed these justifications. Opposition parties, civil society organizations and international watchdogs accuse the government of seeking to undermine the independence of the broadcasters, whose critical reporting has long irked ANO and the SPD in particular. Analysts point out that while models in other EU states include guarantees of long-term financial stability and editorial independence, the Czech government proposal offers neither. CT and CRo have warned that the reduced budget included in the bill will mean programming- and staff cuts . When the first publication of the proposed bill was met with protests over the summer, Vaclav Stetka of the European New School of Digital Studies told DW that such "dramatic budget cuts represent an act of cultural vandalism." There has also been condemnation of the restriction of the parliamentary debate amid the fast-tracking of the bill. The protests continued in the days after the late-night vote in parliament Image: Michael Heitmann/dpa/picture alliance "The confrontational approach, the attempts to limit parliamentary debate and the government's rhetoric towards journalists and critics have all contributed to the public backlash," Otto Eibl, political scientist at Masaryk University in Czechia 's second city Brno, told DW. What has happened since the bill was fast-tracked? The backlash was immediate. Crowds picketed parliament through the night as the government pushed through the first reading of the bill. Since then, multiple rallies have taken place in cities and towns across the country. Many of these protests were led by students and joined by unions, Churches and representatives of educational and cultural institutions. CT and CRo staff called a strike in early November, disrupting the country's TV and radio schedules. Sunday's protest is set to up the ante. It will take place two days before the anniversary of the start of the Velvet Revolution, which ultimately brought down communism in what was then Czechoslovakia in 1989. The civil society group Million Moments for Democracy, which is organizing Sunday's rally, brought an estimated 300,000 onto the streets to protest during Babis's first term as prime minister in 2019 and more than 200,000 earlier this year . Why has the reaction been so strong? The government's sudden bid to push through the proposal reflects impatience to deliver on a core pledge made ahead of the October 2025 election, as well as the longstanding ambition of the prime minister, who was stymied in his attempt to engineer control of CT's governing council during his first term in power in 2017–21. 'For you, not for politicians' — Public broadcasters are seen by many in Czechia as cornerstones of democracy Image: Eva Korinkova/REUTERS Vaclav Stetka notes that repeated assaults on public media by Czech governments past and present reflect a particular political culture across Europe's post-communist states. "The political elite has never accepted the independence of public media," he asserted. In Czechia, however, the public broadcasters have earned special status as cornerstones of democracy . That standing was forged in what became known as the "Czech TV crisis" of 2000–01, when an occupation of CT's studios by staff and mass protests forced the government of the day to back down on a bid to wrest control. "The fight over the public service media has become a symbol of the defense of liberal democratic values and institutions," Eibl said. How has the government reacted? As anger has swelled, the government has sought to calm the situation. Babis has said that a new proposal, which would see public media funding moved off budget and editorial independence guaranteed, would be drawn up and made available for a full and open debate. During the November 3 strike at Czech Television, hosts read the news in front of a darkened newsroom Image: Eva Korinkova/REUTERS However, critics remain unimpressed, noting a lack of any detail and the fact that other members of the government appear determined to remain on course. Million Moments for Democracy has insisted the pressure must continue. "Words are worth nothing," the group said. "While people stand up for independent media, the government continues to act as if it owns the country." What are the potential risks for the government? With little sign that the opposition will dissipate, the government faces a choice. It has the parliamentary majority it needs to push the bill through and defeat any likely vetoes from the upper house Senate and President Petr Pavel . But this could come at a cost. Polls suggest political support for the government has been weakened and could diminish further if the protests expand to include growing frustrations over the cost of living and housing, as happened recently with student-led protests in France and other European countries . "The real risk for the government is that the media issue becomes a lightning rod for broader dissatisfaction," said Martin Vokalek of the Prague-based EUROPEUM Institute for European Policy. Could things turn violent? Babis is aware of the danger. Public opposition to the government's plans for Czech public media are nothing new: this demonstration outside Czech Television in June called for the dismissal of Culture Minister Oto Klempir and expressed support for the country's public media Image: Ondrej Deml/CTK/picture alliance The PM announced that he will not attend the Velvet Revolution anniversary celebrations on November 17, which are hugely symbolic, in the hope that his absence might "calm the tense situation." However, there's little concern that the Czech protests could descend into violence. Analysts note that the anger in Czechia remains tightly focused on the public media proposal and continues to be expressed in a similar way to the seismic events of the country's modern history. "I would not expect French-style scenes," Vokalek told DW, noting that the same "large, peaceful and civic Czech protest culture," which gave the Velvet Revolution and 1993's Velvet Divorce from Slovakia their name, is still strong.
